chapter_title: Reading Digital and Analog Sensors with Arduino

screens.title: Reading Digital and Analog Sensors with Arduino
screens.subtitle: How sensors become the eyes and ears of an IoT device

narration.text: Sensors turn physical signals—temperature, light, motion—into electrical values the Arduino can read. In this lesson you will learn the difference between digital sensors that report HIGH or LOW and analog sensors that return a range of values via analogRead. You will see practical examples: a pushbutton and internal pull-up to read a button press; a TMP36 temperature sensor and the math to convert voltage into degrees Celsius; an LDR in a voltage divider to measure light; and simple filtering like averaging and a median filter to reduce noisy readings. We will also cover calibration methods so your readings map to real-world units, and threshold detection with hysteresis to avoid rapid switching. Each topic includes a short code example or sketch you can run in the Arduino IDE and a hands-on activity that combines three sensors on a breadboard. By the end you’ll understand how to read raw values, convert them to useful units, and make decisions reliably when sensors are noisy. How might you apply these steps to a simple room-monitoring project?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Reading and converting sensor signals correctly is the foundation of reliable IoT systems: accurate readings enable correct decisions, and filtering plus hysteresis prevents false triggers.

screens.title: Digital Sensors: binary signals and reliable reads
screens.subtitle: How switches and motion sensors report events to an Arduino

narration.text: Digital sensors deliver binary information: either HIGH or LOW. This makes them ideal for event detection — a door is open or closed, motion detected or not, a magnet present or not. A pushbutton is the simplest example: when pressed it connects a pin to ground or power. But a common pitfall is leaving the pin floating when the switch is open. That is why we use the Arduino's internal pull-up resistor by configuring a pin as INPUT_PULLUP. The pull-up holds the pin at a defined HIGH level when the button is not pressed; pressing the button then pulls the pin LOW. A practical example is toggling an LED and printing a message to the Serial Monitor when a button press is detected. A misconception is thinking that an open pin reads reliably—floating pins produce random readings and false events. To test this, wire a pushbutton to pin 2 with the other side to ground and set pinMode to INPUT_PULLUP. Then read digitalRead and look for LOW when pressed. For robustness, add a short delay or a debounce routine because mechanical switches can generate very fast, short pulses. Reflect on how the binary nature of digital sensors simplifies detection but requires careful wiring and pull-ups to be reliable. How will you check for pin bouncing in your circuit?

keyIdea.title: Digital reads need defined states
keyIdea.text: Use INPUT_PULLUP to avoid floating pins; expect LOW when a button wired to ground is pressed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Digital Sensors
Core Concept
Binary signals and pull-ups
Digital sensors output HIGH or LOW. INPUT_PULLUP keeps an unused input at HIGH until a switch connects it to ground.
Common mistakes
  • Leaving inputs floating causes random HIGH/LOW reads.
  • Forgetting debounce leads to multiple false triggers on a single press.
Key Takeaway
Define pin state with INPUT_PULLUP and treat LOW as pressed when wired to ground.
Concrete example
const int buttonPin = 2;
const int ledPin = 13;

void setup() {
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  int buttonState = digitalRead(buttonPin);
  if (buttonState == LOW) {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
    Serial.println("Button pressed!");
  } else {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
  }
  delay(50);  // Simple debounce
}
Analogy: pull-up is like a spring that holds the state until you press the button.
Check: if Serial prints without pressing, you likely have a wiring issue or no pull-up.

screens.title: Reading a pushbutton reliably and debouncing
screens.subtitle: From wiring to stable readings in code

narration.text: Reading a pushbutton reliably requires three steps: correct wiring, a defined pin state, and debouncing in software. Start by wiring one side of the button to a digital pin and the other side to ground. In setup, call pinMode with INPUT_PULLUP to enable the internal resistor. This avoids floating. In loop, read the pin with digitalRead and interpret LOW as pressed when wired to ground. However, mechanical switches bounce — they produce quick transitions for a few milliseconds when changing state. A simple mitigation is to sample every short interval and ignore very fast toggles; the provided sketch uses delay(50) as a simple debounce. A more robust pattern stores the last stable reading and only accepts a new state if it remains consistent for a debounce window, typically 10–50 milliseconds. Concrete example: count a button press only when the reading changes and stays different for 30 milliseconds. A common misconception is that delay-based debouncing always works; it can block other work. For non-blocking behavior use a timestamp check and only change state after consistent samples. Try writing a non-blocking debounce and ask: how would you count long presses versus short taps?

keyIdea.title: Debounce matters
keyIdea.text: Mechanical bounce creates multiple transitions; require a stable reading for a short window before accepting a state change to avoid false events.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Button Debounce
Process Flow
Wire → Pull-up → Read → Debounce
  1. Wire button: pin to one side, ground to the other.
  2. Enable pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) so open state is HIGH.
  3. Read digitalRead(pin) and treat LOW as pressed.
  4. Debounce: require a stable read for a short window before accepting a change.
Pro tip
Use a non-blocking timestamp method if your loop must do other tasks while debouncing.
Non-blocking debounce pattern (concept)
// Concept: check time, accept new state only after stable interval
int lastState = HIGH;
unsigned long lastChange = 0;
const unsigned long debounceMs = 30;

void loop() {
  int reading = digitalRead(buttonPin);
  if (reading != lastState) {
    lastChange = millis();
  }
  if ((millis() - lastChange) > debounceMs) {
    // state has been stable for debounceMs
    // handle stable state change here
  }
  lastState = reading;
}
Example: count presses by incrementing a counter when a stable LOW is detected.
Misconception: delay-based debounce blocks sensor reads and is bad for multitasking.

screens.title: Other digital sensors: PIR, Hall, tilt, reed
screens.subtitle: Event types, wiring notes, and when to use each

narration.text: Beyond pushbuttons, several common digital sensors are useful in IoT. PIR motion sensors output HIGH when they detect movement; they often have adjustable sensitivity and a duration output and are good for occupancy detection. A Hall effect sensor reports HIGH when a magnetic field is near, useful for reed-replacement or rotary encoders. Tilt sensors are simple switches that change state with orientation; they are cheap and good for detecting falls or tamper. Reed switches close in the presence of a magnet and are widely used in door and window sensors. When comparing these sensors, consider their response time, mechanical wear, and mounting requirements. For example, PIRs require warm-up and can produce false positives from fast thermal changes; Hall sensors are solid-state and reliable for repeated events. A common misconception is assuming every digital sensor can be read the same way — some need pull-downs, some produce open-collector outputs, and some need a stable supply and a ground reference. Always check the sensor's wiring and provide the correct pull-up or pull-down. Practice: connect a PIR and observe the HIGH pulses and try adjusting sensitivity to see the effect on detection range. Which sensor will you choose for a low-power door sensor?

keyIdea.title: Choose sensors by event and reliability
keyIdea.text: Match sensor characteristics like mechanical wear, response time, and mounting needs to the application; not all digital sensors behave identically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Digital Sensor Comparison
Sensor cards
PIR motion: HIGH on motion, needs warm-up; good for occupancy detection.
Hall effect: solid-state magnetic sensor; reliable for repeated triggers.
Tilt sensor: mechanical switch changes with angle; simple orientation detection.
Reed switch: magnet-activated contact; common in door sensors and low-power designs.
Wiring and caveats

  • Watch for noise and false triggers from environmental changes, especially on PIR sensors.
  • Mechanical sensors may wear; solid-state sensors last longer for frequent events.
Example exercise

screens.title: Analog sensors and analogRead()
screens.subtitle: How analog voltages map to numeric counts

narration.text: Analog sensors output a voltage proportional to a physical quantity. The Arduino's analogRead converts that voltage into a 10-bit number between 0 and 1023. By definition, 0 maps to 0 volts and 1023 maps to the board's reference voltage, commonly 5.0 volts or 3.3 volts depending on the model. To convert a raw reading to a voltage use the formula reading divided by 1023 times the reference voltage. For example, voltage = (analogRead(pin) / 1023.0) * 5.0 on a 5-volt board. This conversion is the first step before applying sensor-specific formulas, like the TMP36 mapping to degrees Celsius. A common misconception is treating analogRead output as a linear physical unit by itself—analogRead is only counts; you must convert to voltage then to the physical unit. Also remember the reference voltage stability matters for accurate conversions. Concrete example: if analogRead returns 512 on a 5V board, the voltage is roughly 2.5 volts. Practice converting readings into volts for different reference voltages and observe how readings scale. How will you verify your reference voltage is stable on your board? Analog sensors and analogRead() means convert analogread counts to voltage using the board reference before mapping to physical units.. In practical terms, how analog voltages map to numeric counts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Counts are not units
keyIdea.text: Convert analogRead counts to voltage using the board reference before mapping to physical units.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Analog Sensors
Definition
analogRead → 0..1023 mapping
The analogRead function returns a 10-bit integer. Convert counts into voltage using the reference voltage before applying sensor-specific formulas.
Formula
voltage = (analogRead(pin) / 1023.0) * Vref
Concrete example
If analogRead(A0) returns 512 and the board is 5V, voltage = (512 / 1023.0) * 5.0 ≈ 2.5V. This voltage is the starting point for sensor conversions.
Check your assumptions
Different Arduino boards use different reference voltages. Confirm Vref before converting.

screens.title: TMP36 temperature sensor: conversion and example
screens.subtitle: How to convert TMP36 voltage into degrees Celsius

narration.text: The TMP36 is an analog temperature sensor that outputs a voltage proportional to temperature. At 25°C it outputs about 750 millivolts, and its scale is 10 millivolts per degree Celsius. The conversion process is two-step: first convert the analogRead count into voltage, then apply the TMP36 formula to compute temperature in Celsius. Concretely: voltage = (analogRead(A0) / 1023.0) * Vref. Then temperatureC = (voltage - 0.5) * 100.0 when using a 5-volt reference and the TMP36 offset. For example, if analogRead returns a value that corresponds to 0.73 volts, the temperature is approximately twenty-three degrees Celsius. A common misconception is forgetting the 500 millivolt offset; subtracting 0.5 before scaling is necessary. In a sketch, perform a small average before conversion to smooth random noise. After computing temperature, print a CSV line with temperature, light percentage, and button state for easy verification in the Serial Monitor. Try comparing the TMP36 reading to a room thermometer to check your calibration. What difference do you observe and how would you correct it? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: TMP36 conversion
keyIdea.text: Convert analogRead to volts, subtract the 0.5V offset, and multiply by 100 to get degrees Celsius.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › TMP36 Conversion
Conversion formula
// Convert analog reading to voltage and degrees C
int raw = analogRead(A0);
float voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * 5.0;
float temperatureC = (voltage - 0.5) * 100.0;
Example: with voltage 0.73, temperature = (0.73 - 0.5) * 100 = 23°C. Remember the 0.5V offset is specific to TMP36.
Practice tip
Take several readings and average them before conversion to reduce random jitter. Compare the final value to a known thermometer for calibration.
Misconception
Do not forget to convert counts to voltage first. Directly scaling counts without accounting for Vref and offset yields wrong temperatures.

screens.title: Voltage divider, LDR and potentiometer patterns
screens.subtitle: Creating a measurable voltage from resistive sensors

narration.text: Many resistive sensors, like LDRs and force-sensitive resistors, change resistance with an environmental parameter. To read them with analogRead you typically build a voltage divider: the sensor and a fixed resistor form two legs between Vcc and ground, producing a measurable middle voltage. The analog pin reads that midpoint voltage. A potentiometer is effectively a built-in three-terminal voltage divider that produces a variable voltage from 0 to Vcc by turning the knob. To convert an LDR reading to a percentage, read the analog value, convert to voltage, and then map that voltage relative to your expected dark and bright references into 0–100%. A practical pitfall is choosing the wrong fixed resistor value for the divider; the resistor should be close to the sensor's resistance at the expected operating point for best sensitivity. Also be aware that the ADC measures voltage, not resistance directly. Concrete example: place an LDR in series with a 10k resistor, read the midpoint, and observe the value change when covering the sensor. How might you pick a better fixed resistor if the LDR value stays near one extreme?

keyIdea.title: Voltage divider principle
keyIdea.text: Sensors that change resistance produce a voltage via a divider; choose the fixed resistor to center the expected range in the ADC span.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Voltage Divider
Architecture
Sensor + fixed resistor → measurable voltage
The ADC reads the midpoint voltage of a divider. For best sensitivity, the fixed resistor should be similar to the sensor resistance at the operating point.
Example setup
LDR in series with 10k resistor; midpoint to A1. Cover the LDR and watch the analogRead change from high to low values.
Convert to percentage
Read raw = analogRead(A1). voltage = (raw / 1023.0) * Vref. Map expected dark and bright voltages to 0–100% for a useful light level.
Pitfall
If sensor values stay near 0 or 1023, change the fixed resistor so the range centers in the ADC span.

screens.title: Calibration: two-point and multi-point methods
screens.subtitle: Turning raw counts into accurate physical units

narration.text: Calibration aligns sensor output to known physical references so measurements are accurate. Two-point calibration measures the sensor output at two known reference points and uses linear interpolation between them. For example, if a temperature sensor gives raw counts of 100 at 0°C and 920 at 100°C, compute a slope in degrees per raw unit and apply it to convert any raw reading. Multi-point calibration collects values across the range and fits a curve or uses a lookup table if the response is non-linear. A concrete two-point example: measure the sensor in ice water for 0°C and boiling water for 100°C, record the raw readings, compute the slope, and apply the linear formula in your sketch. A common misconception is assuming factory output is already accurate; sensors have tolerances and environmental effects, so calibration reduces systematic error. Also remember to calibrate under the same conditions you will operate, because temperature and voltage reference shifts affect results. After calibrating, validate by comparing to reliable references and consider storing calibration constants for reproducible results. What simple two points will you use to check your sensor?

keyIdea.title: Calibration reduces systematic error
keyIdea.text: Two-point calibration is simple and effective for near-linear sensors; multi-point fits handle non-linear responses.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Calibration
Two-point calibration
Measure two known references
Record raw readings at two known physical points, compute slope and intercept, then apply the linear conversion in code.
// Two-point calibration example
// At 0°C raw = 100
// At 100°C raw = 920
float calibrateTemperature(int raw) {
  float slope = 100.0 / (920.0 - 100.0);
  return (raw - 100.0) * slope;
}
Multi-point calibration
Collect multiple reference pairs and fit a polynomial or build a lookup table for non-linear sensors. Validate with independent references.
Practical note
Store calibration constants in EEPROM or in code so you don't need to recalibrate every run.

screens.title: Filtering sensor data: averaging, median, exponential
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between smoothing and responsiveness

narration.text: Real-world sensors are noisy. Filtering reduces noise but introduces trade-offs. Averaging N samples reduces random noise by roughly the square root of N, which is simple to implement: take N analogRead samples and compute the mean. The median filter sorts samples and selects the middle value; it is robust against outliers and spikes. For example, with samples [102, 105, 300, 107, 103], the median is 105 because the outlier 300 is ignored. An exponential moving average (EMA) performs a weighted update: filtered = alpha * current + (1 - alpha) * filtered. A small alpha smooths more but slows response. Each method has use cases: averaging for random jitter, median for spike resistance, EMA for memory-efficient smoothing with tunable responsiveness. A common misconception is that more smoothing is always better; too much smoothing masks real events. When you design thresholds, consider the filtered signal's dynamics so detection remains timely. Try implementing a 10-sample average for temperature and a median filter for light readings to compare responsiveness. Which filter gives the best compromise for your application? Filtering sensor data: averaging, median, exponential means averaging reduces random noise, median resists spikes, and ema offers tunable smoothing with minimal memory.. In practical terms, trade-offs between smoothing and responsiveness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose filters by noise type
keyIdea.text: Averaging reduces random noise, median resists spikes, and EMA offers tunable smoothing with minimal memory.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Filtering
Averaging
Take N samples, sum them, divide by N. Reduces random noise by sqrt(N) but increases latency.
Median filter example
Samples: [102, 105, 300, 107, 103] → sorted [102,103,105,107,300] → median 105. Outliers are ignored.
Exponential moving average
filtered = alpha * current + (1 - alpha) * filtered. Low memory, tunable response. Use alpha between 0 and 1.
Pitfall: too large a smoothing factor delays real changes. Pick alpha to balance noise reduction and responsiveness.
Key Takeaway

Match your filter to the noise type: use median for spikes, averaging for random jitter, and EMA for efficient smoothing with tunable speed.

screens.title: Threshold detection and hysteresis
screens.subtitle: Trigger actions without rapid on/off toggling

narration.text: Threshold detection triggers actions when a sensor value crosses a boundary. A naive single threshold may lead to rapid toggling if the sensor value hovers near that point. Hysteresis solves this by using two thresholds: one to turn on and a different one to turn off, separated by a gap. For example, if you want to turn on a light when lightLevel 500, use a lowThreshold of 300 and a highThreshold of 500. Maintain a boolean state like lightOn and only change it when the corresponding condition is met. This prevents flicker when the measurement hovers around a single threshold. Implement hysteresis after filtering to avoid reacting to raw noisy samples. A common misconception is that tiny hysteresis gaps are enough; choose a gap based on measurement variance. Practically, run the system, plot or watch the raw and filtered readings, and adjust thresholds so the system reacts reliably without excessive delay. What hysteresis gap would you choose for a noisy outdoor light sensor? Threshold detection and hysteresis means use separate on/off thresholds and a maintained state to prevent rapid toggling when sensor values hover near a boundary.. In practical terms, trigger actions without rapid on/off toggling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hysteresis prevents flicker
keyIdea.text: Use separate on/off thresholds and a maintained state to prevent rapid toggling when sensor values hover near a boundary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Hysteresis
Process
Low threshold → turn on. High threshold → turn off.
Maintain state. Only change when the corresponding threshold condition is met to avoid toggling when values bounce near the threshold.
Example thresholds: lowThreshold = 300, highThreshold = 500. Use filtered readings to decide.
Example code snippet
const int lowThreshold = 300;
const int highThreshold = 500;
bool lightOn = false;

void loop() {
  int lightLevel = analogRead(A0);
  if (!lightOn && lightLevel < lowThreshold) {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
    lightOn = true;
  } else if (lightOn && lightLevel > highThreshold) {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
    lightOn = false;
  }
}
Choose thresholds based on filtered measurement variance; larger variance needs a wider hysteresis gap.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Summarize and internalize three core ideas. First, digital sensors are binary and require defined pin states; use INPUT_PULLUP and debounce to avoid false events. Second, analogRead returns counts that must be converted to voltage and then to physical units—apply sensor-specific formulas like TMP36's offset and scaling. Third, real sensor data is noisy: use averaging, median filters, or exponential smoothing and implement hysteresis for threshold-based actions. Each of these concepts addresses a different source of error: wiring and floating pins cause false events; ignoring conversion yields meaningless numbers; unfiltered noise causes flicker and instability. Practice wiring the TMP36, LDR, and pushbutton together, read and average samples, calibrate using known references, and observe how hysteresis stabilizes decisions. Keep these ideas in mind when designing IoT inputs so your device reads the world reliably. Which of these three will you focus on first in your next test?

keyIdea.title: Core recap
keyIdea.text: Digital reliability, analog conversion, and noise handling are the pillars of dependable sensor-based IoT.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
Digital sensors
Use pull-ups and debounce so binary signals are stable and reliable for event detection.
Analog conversion
Convert analogRead counts to voltage, then apply sensor formulas or calibration to get physical units.
Filtering & hysteresis
Reduce noise with averaging, median, or EMA, and use hysteresis to avoid rapid on/off when detecting thresholds.
Summary

Accurate sensor readings come from correct wiring, proper conversion and calibration, and thoughtful noise management—together they make sensor-driven decisions dependable.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to use while prototyping

narration.text: Keep three compact reminders on your bench. First, always define digital pin states; prefer INPUT_PULLUP for buttons wired to ground and add debouncing when counting presses. Second, always convert analogRead to voltage with the correct reference before mapping to °C or percent; verify the TMP36 offset of 0.5 volts and apply the scale. Third, filter aggressively enough to remove noise but not so much that you lose responsiveness; use median filters to ignore spikes and hysteresis to stabilize threshold actions. These short rules will help you debug quickly and make early prototypes behave more like finished products. When you return to your circuit later, follow this checklist: wiring, conversion, filtering, thresholds. Which checklist item will you keep at eye level during your next build? Key Concepts — Quick Reference means wiring, convert-to-units, filter, and use hysteresis—follow this order to build dependable sensor systems.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to use while prototyping. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bench checklist
keyIdea.text: Wiring, convert-to-units, filter, and use hysteresis—follow this order to build dependable sensor systems.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Quick Reference
INPUT_PULLUP
Prevent floating inputs and read buttons reliably; expect LOW when pressed to ground.
TMP36 formula
temperatureC = (voltage - 0.5) * 100. Convert counts to volts first.
Hysteresis rule
Use separate on/off thresholds and track state to avoid flicker near the boundary.
Final takeaway

A small set of wiring and code practices turns noisy raw readings into reliable inputs for any IoT project.
